```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, include=FALSE}
library(shiny)
library(gradethis)
library(learnr)
library(reticulate)

# Exercises graded on a value instead of the exact code. Every exercise with a
# Submit button needs an entry here (and a -check chunk, which enables the button).
# The student's code and the -solution chunk are each run after the exercise's setup
# chunks, and the value from each is compared:
#   list(last_value = TRUE): the value of the last line (or the variable it assigns).
#     print(x) counts as x.
#   list(all_values = TRUE): the value of every bare line, in order.
#   list(var = ...): these variables, which the student's code must assign itself
#     (not just rely on setup).
#   list(expr = "..."): this Python expression, evaluated after the code runs (e.g. a
#     list the code changes in place).
#   list(error = "TypeError"): the student's code must raise this error (no solution needed).
#   structure = ...: rules the code must also follow (see check_structure below), so
#     that e.g. typing the answer (True) doesn't pass a question about an operator.
# Strings, Booleans, types, lists vs tuples must match exactly; numbers must be close,
# and if the solution gives a float the student's answer has to be a float too.
# Any exercise not listed is graded by exact code match against its -solution chunk.
value_checks <- list(
  ex2 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex3 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex9 = list(all_values = TRUE),
  ex11 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex12 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex13 = list(var = "Chewbacca"),
  ex14 = list(var = "Chewbacca"),
  ex15 = list(var = c("Chewbacca", "Luke", "C3PO", "R2D2", "Leia", "Han")),
  ex16 = list(last_value = TRUE, structure = "compare"),
  ex17 = list(last_value = TRUE, structure = "compare"),
  ex18 = list(last_value = TRUE, structure = c("compare", "or")),
  ex19 = list(last_value = TRUE, structure = c("compare", "and")),
  ex21 = list(last_value = TRUE, structure = "compare"),
  ex22 = list(last_value = TRUE, structure = "compare"),
  ex23 = list(var = "leia_lower", structure = "compare"),
  ex24 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex26 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex28 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex29 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex30 = list(error = "TypeError")
)

# Python helpers for custom_checker (done in Python so they work the same on every
# Python version). Each run starts from a fresh namespace with only the exercise's
# setup chunks run in it, so the student's code and the solution can't affect each
# other (or leftovers from other exercises), even when the code changes data in place.
# get_result runs the code and returns the value being checked.
# check_structure returns "" if the code follows every rule, otherwise what is missing.
# raises says whether the code raises the named error.
# values_match compares a student's result to the expected one.
checker_py <- '
def fresh_namespace(setup):
    import builtins
    if setup is None:
        # Setup chunks unavailable, so fall back on a copy of what learnr just ran
        import __main__
        return dict(__main__.__dict__)
    g = {"__name__": "__main__", "__builtins__": builtins}
    for chunk in setup:
        exec(compile(chunk, "<setup>", "exec"), g)
    return g

def get_result(code, setup=None, var=None, expr=None, last_value=False, all_values=False):
    import ast
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    if not tree.body:
        raise ValueError("no code")
    g = fresh_namespace(setup)
    values = []
    for stmt in tree.body:
        if isinstance(stmt, ast.Expr):
            node = stmt.value
            # print(x) shows the same thing as a bare x
            if (isinstance(node, ast.Call) and isinstance(node.func, ast.Name) and node.func.id == "print"
                    and len(node.args) == 1 and not node.keywords):
                node = node.args[0]
            values.append(eval(compile(ast.Expression(node), "<exercise>", "eval"), g))
        else:
            exec(compile(ast.Module([stmt], type_ignores=[]), "<exercise>", "exec"), g)
    if expr is not None:
        return eval(expr, g)
    if all_values:
        if not values:
            raise ValueError("no values")
        return values
    if last_value:
        last = tree.body[-1]
        if isinstance(last, ast.Expr):
            return values[-1]
        if isinstance(last, ast.Assign) and len(last.targets) == 1 and isinstance(last.targets[0], ast.Name):
            # Last line is `name = expr`, so read `name`
            return g[last.targets[0].id]
        raise ValueError("last line is not an expression")
    # The variables have to be assigned by the student, not just left over from setup
    assigned = {n.id for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Name) and isinstance(n.ctx, ast.Store)}
    names = [var] if isinstance(var, str) else list(var)
    for name in names:
        if name not in assigned or name not in g:
            raise NameError(name + " not defined")
    return g[var] if isinstance(var, str) else [g[name] for name in names]

def check_structure(code, rules=()):
    import ast
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    nodes = list(ast.walk(tree))
    for rule in rules:
        if rule == "compare":
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.Compare) for n in nodes):
                return "Make sure to use a comparison operator."
        elif rule in ("or", "and"):
            op = ast.Or if rule == "or" else ast.And
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.BoolOp) and isinstance(n.op, op) for n in nodes):
                return "Make sure to use the `" + rule + "` operator."
        elif rule == "no_literal":
            last = tree.body[-1] if tree.body else None
            node = last.value if isinstance(last, ast.Expr) else None
            if isinstance(node, ast.Call) and isinstance(node.func, ast.Name) and node.func.id == "print" and len(node.args) == 1:
                node = node.args[0]
            if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp):
                node = node.operand
            if isinstance(node, ast.Constant):
                return "Use code to find the answer instead of typing it in."
        else:
            raise ValueError("unknown structure rule: " + rule)
    return ""

def raises(code, error, setup=None):
    import builtins
    g = fresh_namespace(setup)
    try:
        exec(compile(code, "<exercise>", "exec"), g)
    except getattr(builtins, error):
        return True
    except Exception:
        return False
    return False

def values_match(actual, expected):
    import math
    import numbers
    try:
        import numpy as np
    except ImportError:
        np = None
    def is_bool(x):
        return isinstance(x, bool) or (np is not None and isinstance(x, np.bool_))
    def match(a, e):
        if np is not None and isinstance(e, np.ndarray):
            if not isinstance(a, np.ndarray) or a.shape != e.shape:
                return False
            try:
                return bool(np.allclose(a, e, equal_nan=True))
            except TypeError:
                return bool(np.array_equal(a, e))
        # Lists and tuples have to be the same kind, with matching elements in order
        if isinstance(e, (list, tuple)):
            return type(a) is type(e) and len(a) == len(e) and all(match(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, e))
        if isinstance(e, dict):
            return isinstance(a, dict) and a.keys() == e.keys() and all(match(a[k], e[k]) for k in e)
        if isinstance(e, (set, frozenset)):
            return isinstance(a, (set, frozenset)) and a == e
        if isinstance(e, type):
            return a is e
        if is_bool(e):
            return is_bool(a) and bool(a) == bool(e)
        if isinstance(e, str):
            return isinstance(a, str) and a == e
        if isinstance(e, numbers.Number):
            if is_bool(a) or not isinstance(a, numbers.Number):
                return False
            # If the answer should be a float (e.g. from float()), an int does not count
            if not isinstance(e, numbers.Integral) and isinstance(a, numbers.Integral):
                return False
            return math.isclose(a, e, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9)
        try:
            return bool(a == e)
        except Exception:
            return False
    return match(actual, expected)
'

# Loads checker_py as its own Python module (so its functions can call each other)
load_checker_py <- function() {
  module <- reticulate::import("types", convert = FALSE)$ModuleType("lab_checker")
  reticulate::import_builtins(convert = FALSE)$exec(checker_py, module$`__dict__`)
  module
}

# The code of the setup chunks learnr ran before this exercise (following any
# exercise.setup chain), found on the learnr exercise that is calling the checker.
# NULL if it can't be found.
exercise_setup_code <- function() {
  for (frame in rev(sys.frames())) {
    ex <- get0("exercise", envir = frame, inherits = FALSE)
    if (is.list(ex) && !is.null(ex$chunks)) {
      chunks <- Filter(function(ch) !identical(ch$label, ex$label), ex$chunks)
      return(lapply(chunks, function(ch) paste(ch$code, collapse = "\n")))
    }
  }
  NULL
}

custom_checker <- function(label, user_code, solution_code, check_code, envir_result, evaluate_result, envir_prep, last_value, stage, ...) {
  # (learnr doesn't pass the last value of Python chunks, so we run the code)
  if (label %in% names(value_checks)) {
    spec <- value_checks[[label]]
    # Code that should raise an error is graded at the "error_check" stage, which
    # learnr runs instead of "check" when the student's code errors
    if (!(stage == "check" || (stage == "error_check" && !is.null(spec$error)))) return()
    setup <- exercise_setup_code()
    structure_msg <- tryCatch({
      helpers <- load_checker_py()
      reticulate::py_to_r(helpers$check_structure(user_code, as.list(spec$structure)))
    }, error = function(e) "")
    if (nzchar(structure_msg)) {
      return(list(message = paste(random_encouragement(), structure_msg), correct = FALSE))
    }
    correct <- tryCatch({
      helpers <- load_checker_py()
      if (!is.null(spec$error)) {
        isTRUE(reticulate::py_to_r(helpers$raises(user_code, spec$error, setup = setup)))
      } else {
        var <- if (length(spec$var) > 1) as.list(spec$var) else spec$var
        get_result <- function(code) {
          helpers$get_result(code, setup = setup, var = var, expr = spec$expr,
                             last_value = isTRUE(spec$last_value), all_values = isTRUE(spec$all_values))
        }
        actual <- get_result(user_code)
        expected <- get_result(solution_code)
        isTRUE(reticulate::py_to_r(helpers$values_match(actual, expected)))
      }
    }, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (correct) {
      return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
    }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
  # Exact code checking (requires a <label>-solution chunk and <label>-code-check chunk)
  if (stage == "code_check") {
      if (user_code == solution_code){
          return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
      }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
}

gradethis_setup()
tutorial_options(exercise.completion = FALSE, exercise.checker = custom_checker, exercise.blanks = "\\.{3}", exercise.reveal_solution = FALSE)
```

## Goals

The goal of this tutorial is to introduce you to the style of tutorials we will be using to learn to program and to review some of what you've learned about basic data types in Python. We will cover:

- Ints
- Floats
- Booleans
- Strings

## How Does This Tutorial Work?

Before we ask you to start working in a Jupyter notebook, we will ask you to complete this tutorial in a web browser so you can get used to one thing at a time.

## Syntax Highlighting

Remember that syntax is "the arrangement of words and phrases to create well-formed sentences in a language", a.k.a., coding grammar. Syntax highlighting displays code in different colors and fonts to help programmers identify different pieces of code quickly. 

The syntax highlighting on my slides is different from the syntax highlighting in this tutorial, which may be different from the syntax highlighting you are using. Let's take a quick look at the syntax highlighting in your tutorial.

## Ints and Floats

Remember that numbers can be stored as `ints` or `floats` in Python. An `int` is a number without a decimal point; a `float` usually has a decimal point (or is stored in scientific notation). Remember also that the `type()` function will tell us what kind of object we are working with. 

Edit the code below to find the types of the numbers:

```{python ex9, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
18
22.7
```

```{python ex9-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
type(18)
type(22.7)
```



Other types have more specific methods, but for ints and floats, we are happy using simple operators or comparison operators. 

| Operation | Operator | Example | Output |
|:---------:|:-----:|:------:|------:|
| Addition | `+` | `2+3` |   `5`   |
| Subtraction | `-` | `2-3` |   `-1`   |
| Multiplication | `*` | `2*3` |   `6`   |
| Division | `/` | `7/3` |   `2.33`   |
| Floor Division | `//` | `7//3` |   `2`   |
| Remainder (mod) | `%` | `7%3` |   `1`   |
| Exponentiation | `**` | `2**0.5` |   `1.41421`   |

Use the cell below to experiment with the operators. Try to use the operators in sequence, with and without parentheses.


Don't forget, there are also the comparison operators:

| Comparison | Operator | True Example | False Example |
|:---------:|:-----:|:------:|------:|
| Less than | `<` | `2 < 3` |   `2 < 2`   |
| Greater than | `>` | `3 > 2` |   `3 > 3`   |
| Less than or equal | `<=` | `2 <= 2 ` |   ` 3 <= 2 `   |
| Greater than or equal | `>=` | `3 >= 3` |   `2 >= 3`   |
| Exactly equal | `==` | `3  == 3` |   `3 == 2`   |
| Not Equal | `!=` | `3 != 2` |   `3 != 3`   |

Use the cell below to experiment with the comparison operators. Using them with `int`s and `float`s should be familiar, but you can also use them with strings and Booleans. 

```{python ex11_0, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}

```

```{r q9, echo=FALSE}
  answer("`False`"),
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

We can use multiple operators, as well as the parentheses, to carry out more advanced calculations. For example, some of you may be familiar with the average or mean:

$$\bar{x} = \frac{x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_n}{n}$$

In other words, to find the average of a variable, you add all the numbers up and divide by the number of observations. 

Consider the heights in centimeters of the following Star Wars characters: 

* Luke Skywalker--172cm
* C-3PO--167cm
* R2-D2--96cm
* Leia Organa--150cm
* Han Solo--180cm, and 
* Chewbacca--238cm

Using the `+` and `/` operators, as well as the parentheses, write a line of code to calculate the average. 

```{python ex11, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}

```

```{python ex11-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
(172+167+96+150+180+238)/6
```

```{r ex11-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```

As we have said, there are not many `int`- and `float`-specific methods, but there are some built-in functions in Python that make working with numbers easier:

| Function | Description |
|:---------:|:-----:|
| `abs()` | Returns the absolute value of a number |
| `float()` | Returns (or converts an object to) a floating point number |
| `int()` | Returns (or converts an object to) an integer number |
| `round()` | Rounds a number |

Convert the integer 172 to a float using one of these functions in the cell below:

```{python ex12, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
172
```

```{python ex12-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
float(172)
```

## Variable Assignment

Let's revisit the heights of the Star Wars characters. Consider Chewbacca in particular--it turns out that his height is 228cm, not 238. If we were correcting a data analysis, we would have to re-type in all those numbers to find the correct mean. However, if you were handing it off to a colleague or if enough time had passed, you may not remember exactly why you wrote what you wrote. 

Sometimes, to make it easier to track our work, we use something called *variable assignment*. Variable assignment helps us store values to work with using a variable name and the *assignment operator*, `=`. 

Consider the following code:

```{python ex13, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
Chewbacca = 238
```

```{python ex13-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
Chewbacca = 228
```

```{r ex13-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```

This time, if you click on the "Run Code" button, it looks like nothing happens. That's not technically true--we corrected the height by re-storing the value, but we can't necessarily see what happened. Another built-in function is the `print()` function. Click on the "Run Code" button below, and then edit Chewbacca's height--does the output change at all?

## Booleans

Now let's practice working with Booleans using our variables, `Chewbacca`, `Luke`, `C3PO`, `R2D2`, `Leia`, and `Han`. Remember that Booleans are outputted by the comparison operators:

| Comparison | Operator | True Example | False Example |
|:---------:|:-----:|:------:|------:|
| Less than | `<` | `2 < 3` |   `2<2`   |
| Greater than | `>` | `3 > 2` |   `3>3`   |
| Less than or equal | `<=` | `2 <=2 ` |   ` 3<=2 `   |
| Greater than or equal | `>=` | `3 >= 3` |   `2 >= 3`   |
| Exactly equal | `==` | `3  == 3` |   `3 == 2`   |
| Not Equal | `!=` | `3 != 2` |   `3 != 3`   |

## Strings

Saving the most complicated for last! Unlike `int`s, `float`s, and Booleans, strings have LOTS of methods we can use. Remember that unlike a function, a method is a tool associated with specific type of object. 

First, let's create a variable for Leia Organa's full name:

```{python ex20, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
Leia_fullname = "Leia Organa"
```

A few things:

1. First, we are choosing separate variable name for Leia's full name--if we saved it as `Leia`, we would lose the information about her height. Be careful in your own work not to overwrite variables unless you really, really mean it!
2. `Leia_fullname` is the name of a variable, whereas `"Leia Organa"` is a string stored as `Leia_fullname`. Remember that strings begin and end with quotation marks, and show up as green, whereas variable names are black. 

Strings are the same whether you use double or single quotes to define them. Write a line of code to see if `Leia_fullname` is the same as `'Leia Organa'` using a comparison operator.


So far, we have only considered fairly short strings, but they can be relatively long, as well! Consider Princess Leia's message to Obi-Wan Kenobi in *A New Hope*. 

```{python ex25, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
message = "General Kenobi. Years ago you served my father in the Clone Wars. Now he begs you to help him in his struggle against the Empire. I regret that I am unable to present my father's request to you in person, but my ship has fallen under attack, and I'm afraid my mission to bring you to Alderaan has failed. I have placed information vital to the survival of the Rebellion into the memory systems of this R2 unit. My father will know how to retrieve it. You must see this droid safely delivered to him on Alderaan. This is our most desperate hour. Help me, Obi-Wan Kenobi. You're my only hope."
```

We might be interested in locating shorter strings within larger strings. For example, we could examine the contents of `message` to find how many times the shorter string `"Kenobi"` appears, but the longer the string, the more difficult this task will be. Instead, let's consider the `.count()` method.
This method is different than many we have seen, because we have to pass what is known as an "argument". An argument is a value that you pass into a function or method--in this case, the argument is the shorter string, `"Kenobi"`. 

We can change the argument. Edit the code below so that we count the number of times the string `"father"` occurs in `message`. 

```{python ex26, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
message.count("Kenobi")
```



In addition to having specific methods, some of the operators we are already familiar with operate differently with strings. Consider the following cells. What happens if you add the two strings together?

```{python ex28, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
obiwan = "These aren't the droids you're looking for."
stormtrooper = "These aren't the droids we're looking for."
...
```

```{python ex28-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}

stormtrooper = "These aren't the droids we're looking for."
obiwan + stormtrooper
```

```{r ex28-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```

When used with strings, the `+` is the concatenation operator. It pastes the two messages together, exactly as they are--notice that there is no space in between the sentences in the concatenated message, even though we would normally put one there. 

What happens if you use the multiplication operator, `*`, with `message_short`? Multiply it by 3.

```{python ex29, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
...
```


You should get an error! Remember that sometimes error messages are frustrating, but they are supposed to help us debug our code. In this case, we got a `TypeError`, because we tried to multiply a string (allowed) by an object of the `float` type (not allowed). The multiplication operator only works with type `int`.
